spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2022 · General Studies Paper II · Q2
spec.text: “Right of movement and residence throughout the territory of India are freely available to the Indian citizens, but these rights are not absolute.” Comment.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-two. General Studies Paper Two, ten marks, one hundred and fifty words. Movement and residence are free for citizens, but not absolute. Comment. Here's the strange part. The Constitution itself says so, in one clause.
scenes.visual: The printed question on a paper card, credit line 'UPSC CSE (Main) 2022, GS Paper II, Q2'. The words 'not absolute' glow (plant).

spec.text: “Right of movement and residence throughout the territory of India are freely available to the Indian citizens, but these rights are not absolute.” Comment.

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Comment means give a view, and back it. There are three jobs. Show the right is free, for citizens. Show its limits. Then give a verdict with cases.
scenes.visual: Question X-ray: 'Comment' highlighted; three empty boxes D1 to D3 (plant: they tick at the end).

spec.title: Free to Move, But Not Absolute (UPSC GS II 2022)

lines.text: Article nineteen, one, d and e, gives citizens free movement and residence.

scenes.vo: Start with the right. Article nineteen, one, d and e, gives citizens free movement and residence. Article nineteen says all citizens. So foreigners cannot claim it.
scenes.visual: A map of India with an open road; a 'citizens' badge on Article 19.

lines.text: But Article nineteen, five, makes it conditional.
A law may impose reasonable restrictions.
Two grounds are named: the general public interest, and Scheduled Tribe interests.

scenes.vo: But Article nineteen, five, makes it conditional. A law may impose reasonable restrictions. Two grounds are named: the general public interest, and Scheduled Tribe interests.
scenes.visual: The clause 19(5) as a paper card; the two grounds light up (plant pays off).

lines.text: But courts watch the word reasonable.
In nineteen fifty-two, Gurbachan Singh upheld externment.
In nineteen fifty-four, Ebrahim Vazir Mavat did not allow a citizen's removal.

scenes.vo: But courts watch the word reasonable. In nineteen fifty-two, Gurbachan Singh upheld externment. In nineteen fifty-four, Ebrahim Vazir Mavat did not allow a citizen's removal. The test is reasonableness.
scenes.visual: Two judgment cards, one with a green tick, one with a red cross; a scale of 'reasonable'.

blocks.text: Article 19(1)(d) and (e) give citizens, not foreigners, free movement and residence in India.
1. The Constitution's limits

• _Article 19(5)_: reasonable restrictions in the general public interest or to protect any Scheduled Tribe. • _Emergency_: Article 358 suspends Article 19 during a war or external-aggression Emergency. • Residence: Article 16(3) lets Parliament require it for some posts.
2. What the courts held

• _Gurbachan Singh_ (1952): externment upheld as a reasonable restriction. • _Ebrahim Vazir Mavat_ (1954): removing a citizen violated Article 19(1)(e). • _Anuradha Bhasin_ (2020): section 144 orders must be necessary and reasoned. • _Maneka Gandhi_ (1978): these freedoms 'are not and cannot be absolute'. • _Amit Sahni_ (2020): a protest cannot block public ways indefinitely.
So the rights are fundamental yet conditional: a restriction must be by law and reasonable.

scenes.vo: Now we write. One hundred and fifty words, about seven minutes. Open with the right and who holds it. One line.

weak.text: Article 19 rights belong to every person in India, including foreigners.
Article 19(5) lets the police stop anyone's movement at will.
weak.miss: a restriction must be by law, reasonable and on two named grounds

weak.text: Externment was struck down in Gurbachan Singh.
weak.miss: the Court upheld it as reasonable

scenes.vo: Now the easy answer beside it. It says Article nineteen belongs to every person. It says all citizens. It says police can stop anyone at will. It says Gurbachan Singh struck externment down. And it names no case.
